Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- From cyberspace to college campuses, many young conservatives are worried that Sen. John McCain is not appealing to their generation. Sen. John McCain says he knows how important young voters are. At a town hall meeting in Ohio this month, a student told McCain that Republicans were a dying breed on his campus. "I understand the challenge I have, and I understand that this election is really all about the people of your generation," McCain said. Many young Republicans said Sen. Barack Obama, the 46-year-old junior senator from Illinois, is inspiring voters their age, but McCain, the 71-year-old Arizona senator who has been in office since the early '80s, is not. Eric Perlmutter, a Republican and student at the at the University of Southern California, said the roaring enthusiasm that follows Obama is missing among conservatives his age. "We try to get people out to our college Republican meetings, but ... we can't seem to draw the same kind of vocal support," he said. At the July town hall meeting in Portsmouth, Ohio, McCain said he knows that he has "a lot of work to do" with the younger voters. The senator said he needs young conservatives to help spread his message for him, because "there's nothing that convinces young people like other young people." McCain also acknowledged the importance of using the Internet to reach out to a generation that stays in touch via social networking sites. On MySpace, Obama has more than 427,000 friends, compared with fewer than 60,000 for McCain. Perlmutter said he cringed when McCain admitted he doesn't use e-mail. Obama, however, is frequently seen with Blackberry in hand. Additionally, Perlmutter pointed out that the images used in McCain's campaign -- such as a message about small businesses showing a barber shop with a traditional red and blue pole -- hardly connect to the younger generation. "Well, when you see the Main Street barber shop image, you think of 1950s America. An entrepreneur, a Silicon Valley guy would definitely make him more attractive," he said. Obama also has increased his college-age appeal by holding rallies and giving speeches at hundreds of campuses. McCain has said he recognizes that he needs to get out to those venues "where young people are engaged and receiving their information and forming their opinions." "Sen. McCain should demand that these same colleges and universities host him or else their tax-exempt status could be in jeopardy," said Jason Mattera, spokesman for Young America's Foundation, a conservative outreach group. McCain must work to connect young voters to conservative principles, Mattera said. "So if they are suspicious of Uncle Sam telling them what Internet sites they can view, they should be equally suspicious of the federal government telling them what health care plan they are going to be a part of," he said. According to a Pew Research Center study conducted between October and March, McCain has a big numbers gap to close. The study found that the current generation of young voters, those who came of age during the President Bush years, are giving the Democrats a wide edge. Fifty-eight percent of voters under 30 identified or leaned toward the Democratic Party, compared with 33 percent who said they identified or leaned toward the Republican Party. The McCain campaign said it plans to increase the senator's presence on sites such as Facebook and MySpace in addition to the candidate making appearance on shows that appeal to younger viewers, such as "The Daily Show with Jon Stewart," "The Tonight Show with Jay Leno" and the "Late Show with David Letterman." In past elections, both parties have tended to put less focus on younger voters because historically, their turnout has been low. With fewer than four months until the November election, McCain said he's confident he can convince young voters that he is the candidate for them. "I believe that I can convince them that I have the plan of action and the ideals and the goals and the inspiration that, as next president of the United States, I can serve better their interests than my opponent," he said.

(CNN) — From cyberspace to college campuses, many young conservatives worry that Sen. John McCain is failing to appeal to their generation.

McCain says he understands the importance of young voters. At a town hall meeting in Ohio this month, a student told him that Republicans were a dying breed on his campus.

“I understand the challenge I have, and I understand that this election is really all about the people of your generation,” McCain said.

Many young Republicans say Sen. Barack Obama, the 46-year-old junior senator from Illinois, inspires voters their age in a way that McCain—the 71-year-old Arizona senator who has held office since the early 1980s—does not.

Eric Perlmutter, a Republican and a student at the University of Southern California, said the fervent enthusiasm surrounding Obama is absent among conservatives his age.

“We try to get people out to our college Republican meetings, but ... we can’t seem to draw the same kind of vocal support,” he said.

At the July town hall meeting in Portsmouth, Ohio, McCain acknowledged that he has “a lot of work to do” with younger voters. He said he needs young conservatives to help spread his message because “there’s nothing that convinces young people like other young people.”

McCain also recognized the importance of using the Internet to reach a generation that stays connected through social networking sites. On MySpace, Obama has more than 427,000 friends, compared with fewer than 60,000 for McCain.

Perlmutter said he cringed when McCain admitted that he does not use e-mail. Obama, by contrast, is frequently seen with a BlackBerry in hand.

Perlmutter also noted that the imagery used in McCain’s campaign—such as a small-business message featuring a barbershop with a traditional red-and-blue pole—hardly resonates with the younger generation.

“Well, when you see the Main Street barber shop image, you think of 1950s America. An entrepreneur, a Silicon Valley guy would definitely make him more attractive,” he said.

Obama has further strengthened his appeal among college-age voters by holding rallies and delivering speeches at hundreds of campuses. McCain has said he recognizes the need to visit venues “where young people are engaged and receiving their information and forming their opinions.”

“Sen. McCain should demand that these same colleges and universities host him or else their tax-exempt status could be in jeopardy,” said Jason Mattera, spokesman for Young America’s Foundation, a conservative outreach group.

Mattera said McCain must work to connect young voters with conservative principles.

“So if they are suspicious of Uncle Sam telling them what Internet sites they can view, they should be equally suspicious of the federal government telling them what health care plan they are going to be a part of,” he said.

According to a Pew Research Center study conducted between October and March, McCain faces a substantial numbers gap. The study found that the current generation of young voters—those who came of age during the President Bush years—strongly favors Democrats.

Fifty-eight percent of voters under 30 identified with or leaned toward the Democratic Party, compared with 33 percent who identified with or leaned toward the Republican Party.

The McCain campaign said it plans to expand the senator’s presence on sites such as Facebook and MySpace. The candidate also plans to appear on programs that appeal to younger viewers, including “The Daily Show with Jon Stewart,” “The Tonight Show with Jay Leno” and the “Late Show with David Letterman.”

In past elections, both parties have tended to focus less on younger voters because their turnout has historically been low.

With fewer than four months remaining before the November election, McCain said he is confident he can persuade young voters that he is the candidate for them.

“I believe that I can convince them that I have the plan of action and the ideals and the goals and the inspiration that, as next president of the United States, I can serve better their interests than my opponent,” he said.

He also argued that McCain’s campaign imagery failed to resonate with younger audiences. For example, a small-business message featured an old-fashioned barbershop with a red-and-blue pole. Obama had further strengthened his support among college-age voters by delivering speeches and holding rallies on hundreds of campuses. McCain said he understood that he needed to visit the places where young people participate, obtain information and develop their views.

He argued that young people who distrust government efforts to control which websites they may visit should likewise question federal control over the health care plan in which they would be enrolled.

With less than four months remaining before the November election, McCain said he was confident he could persuade young people that he was the better choice. Although many support the Republican nominee’s positions on national security, taxes, and limited government, they fear that his campaign’s style and methods appear out of step with the way younger Americans communicate and participate in politics.

In response, McCain’s campaign has begun looking for ways to reach young voters through their peers rather than relying solely on traditional campaign events and television advertising. His image is shaped by a long career in Washington, and his limited familiarity with digital technology reinforces the impression that he is distant from the daily experiences of younger Americans. Even when his campaign adopts online tools, critics worry that its efforts can feel cautious, formal, or dated rather than spontaneous and participatory.

Messages centered on fiscal responsibility, entrepreneurship, personal freedom, and national service could appeal to younger voters, but only if they are communicated through the platforms and voices that young people trust. That means allowing younger activists to take a more visible role and giving them enough freedom to create content that feels authentic.

If Democrats continue to dominate youth enthusiasm and online organizing, they may build political loyalties that last well beyond a single election. counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about John McCain’s struggle to appeal to young voters during the 2008 presidential campaign, especially compared with Barack Obama.
counterfactuals.output:
# McCain struggles to close Obama’s commanding youth-vote advantage

**By CNN Political Unit**  
**October 2008**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — At 72, Sen. John McCain has built his presidential campaign around decades of experience, a reputation for political independence and a compelling biography as a Navy pilot and prisoner of war.

But among the nation’s youngest voters, those credentials have struggled to compete with Sen. Barack Obama’s promise of generational change.

Throughout the 2008 campaign, Obama has enjoyed a wide advantage among voters under 30, drawing enormous crowds on college campuses and building an online organizing network that has turned Facebook profiles, text messages and small-dollar donations into political muscle.

McCain, by contrast, has often appeared more comfortable in town-hall meetings than in the fast-moving digital spaces where many young voters get their news and connect with campaigns.

The challenge is not simply one of age. It is also about issues and political identity.

Many young voters oppose the war in Iraq, while McCain has been one of the conflict’s most prominent defenders and a leading supporter of the troop surge. Obama, who opposed the invasion before entering the Senate, has repeatedly used that contrast to argue that he offers a break from Washington’s past.

The economy has added to McCain’s difficulties. As the financial crisis deepens, younger Americans are increasingly worried about college costs, student debt, health insurance and finding work after graduation. Obama has sought to link those concerns to his plans for expanded college assistance, health care reform and middle-class tax relief.

McCain has tried to make inroads. He has emphasized national service, climate change and government reform — issues with potential appeal beyond the traditional Republican base. His campaign has also pointed to his willingness to challenge his own party, including on immigration and campaign finance.

His life story can resonate with young audiences, particularly when he speaks about sacrifice and public service. And some young conservatives say McCain’s national security experience offers reassurance during uncertain times.

Still, the contrast in campaign culture has been difficult to overcome.

Obama’s organization has treated young people not merely as an audience but as volunteers, donors and organizers. Supporters have used social-networking tools to plan events, register voters and recruit friends. The campaign’s decision to announce Obama’s vice presidential choice by text message underscored its effort to present itself as technologically fluent and connected to a new generation.

McCain’s campaign has expanded its own online outreach, but it has not matched Obama’s scale or enthusiasm. Television images of Obama speaking before packed arenas have reinforced the perception that his candidacy is part of a broader youth movement.

The stakes are significant. Young voters have historically turned out at lower rates than older Americans, but they could become decisive if Obama’s campaign converts its enthusiasm into ballots, particularly in closely contested states with large college populations.

McCain’s path depends in part on persuading those voters that experience matters more than novelty — and that his record of independence represents its own form of change.

But as Election Day approaches, the burden remains on the Republican nominee. Obama has become the overwhelming favorite of young voters, while McCain is still trying to convince them that a candidate from an older generation can speak to their future.

counterfactuals.output:
During the 2008 campaign, many College Republicans said John McCain was having difficulty generating the enthusiasm among young conservatives that Barack Obama was creating among young Democrats and independents.

Students generally respected McCain’s military service, experience and willingness to depart from party orthodoxy. But some described his campaign as remote and uninspiring, saying he spoke more naturally about national security and fiscal restraint than about college costs, jobs, technology and other issues affecting their generation. Several said they expected to vote for him largely because he was the Republican nominee—or because they opposed Obama—rather than from strong personal enthusiasm. Others worried that McCain’s age, conventional campaign style and sometimes strained relationship with the conservative movement made it harder for him to connect on campuses.

Conservative activists echoed those concerns. They argued that McCain lacked both Obama’s youthful image and the organizational energy that had surrounded earlier conservative campaigns. Some urged him to communicate more through the internet and social media, appear more often on campuses, and give young Republicans an affirmative cause rather than relying on his biography or criticism of the Democratic nominee. At the same time, activists noted that McCain’s support for the Iraq war, campaign-finance regulation and immigration legislation had alienated portions of the conservative base that normally supplied campus volunteers.

McCain acknowledged the problem. He joked repeatedly about his age—calling himself “older than dirt” and saying he had “more scars than Frankenstein”—while insisting that experience and character mattered more than youth. He also conceded that Obama had an exceptional ability to attract and motivate young voters. McCain said he intended to compete for them by emphasizing service, national security, climate change and reform, and by pointing to his own record of challenging Washington.

The broader concern was not necessarily that young Republicans would defect in large numbers. Rather, students and activists feared they would vote without volunteering, donating or persuading friends—leaving McCain without the energized campus network Obama was building.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a political news story examining the generational gap between McCain and Obama, with discussion of social media, campus outreach, campaign imagery, and youth polling data.
counterfactuals.output:
## Obama-McCain contest exposed a widening generational divide

**WASHINGTON —** The 2008 presidential campaign was not simply a contest between two parties. It was also a collision between political generations.

At 72, Republican Sen. John McCain presented himself as an experienced national-security leader whose biography was rooted in military service, Vietnam and decades in the Senate. At 47, Democratic Sen. Barack Obama offered a message of generational change, delivered through social networks, college campuses and campaign imagery designed to look more like a movement than a traditional political organization.

The 25-year age difference was visible in their policies and presentation, but nowhere was it more pronounced than among young voters. National exit polls showed Obama defeating McCain by roughly 66% to 32% among voters ages 18 to 29. Four years earlier, Democrat John Kerry had carried the same age group by a much narrower margin.

Young voters were not merely more Democratic than the electorate as a whole; they became a central part of Obama’s campaign infrastructure. His organization used Facebook, text messages, email and its My.BarackObama.com platform to recruit volunteers, promote events and encourage supporters to contact friends. Rather than relying only on television advertising or local party organizations, the campaign gave supporters digital tools to organize on their own.

McCain’s campaign also maintained an online presence, but its public identity remained more closely tied to town-hall meetings, television appearances and the candidate’s personal story. The contrast sometimes made McCain appear to be running a conventional campaign against an opponent building a political network.

That difference was especially apparent on college campuses. Obama organizers registered students, established campus chapters and used peer-to-peer appeals to turn rallies into volunteer drives. Campaign events near universities frequently drew large crowds, creating photographs and television footage that reinforced the candidate’s image as the leader of a rising generation.

McCain reached out to younger voters through student groups, national-security arguments and appeals to service. His campaign emphasized independence from his party and his record of challenging Washington. But those themes competed with widespread dissatisfaction over the Iraq war, the economy and President George W. Bush, whose approval ratings were especially weak among younger Americans.

The candidates’ visual messages deepened the divide. Obama’s rising-sun logo, Shepard Fairey’s “HOPE” poster and images of racially diverse crowds conveyed novelty and optimism. The campaign’s polished videos and shareable graphics were well suited to an emerging online culture.

McCain’s “Country First” slogan and campaign imagery stressed sacrifice, patriotism and tested leadership. Photographs often highlighted his military record, his years as a prisoner of war and his reputation for resilience. To supporters, those images communicated experience in dangerous times. To some younger voters, however, they belonged to a political era they knew largely through history books.

The gap was about more than style. Polling during the campaign found younger Americans more likely to oppose the Iraq war, favor government action on climate change and support a larger role for Washington in expanding health coverage. The financial crisis further strengthened Obama’s argument that the country needed a break with existing leadership.

Youth turnout also increased. The Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement estimated that about half of eligible voters under 30 cast ballots in 2008, with roughly 23 million young Americans participating. Their overwhelming support gave Obama millions more votes than McCain within that age group.

Still, the generational divide should not be reduced to age alone. McCain attracted young conservatives, military families and voters who valued his record, while Obama won support from many older Americans. Nor did digital campaigning replace traditional organization: Obama’s online operation worked because it was connected to field offices, volunteers and door-to-door canvassing.

But the election demonstrated that campaign technology and campaign identity had become inseparable. Obama’s advantage among young voters reflected both his positions and the way his organization allowed supporters to participate.

McCain asked voters to trust a lifetime of service. Obama asked them to see themselves as part of a new political generation. In 2008, young Americans answered that appeal with one of the most lopsided age-group results in modern presidential politics.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: How did John McCain’s limited Internet presence and older public image affect his support among voters under 30 in the 2008 election? Answer in the form of a detailed CNN report.
counterfactuals.output:
# McCain’s digital gap and older image hurt him with young voters in 2008

**WASHINGTON (CNN-style report)** — John McCain entered the 2008 presidential race with decades of experience, a reputation for independence and a compelling biography as a Vietnam prisoner of war. But among voters under 30, those strengths were overwhelmed by a generational contrast that played out both online and on the campaign trail.

National exit polls showed Barack Obama winning voters ages 18 to 29 by roughly **66% to 32%**, one of the widest youth-vote margins in modern presidential politics. Four years earlier, President George W. Bush had received about 45% of that age group. McCain’s decline reflected broader political forces, but his comparatively weak digital operation and his image as an older, traditional politician made it harder for him to reverse the trend.

## Obama campaigned where younger voters lived

By 2008, young adults were increasingly getting political information through the Internet, social-networking sites, online video and text messages. Obama’s campaign treated those tools as central organizing infrastructure rather than as supplements to television advertising and conventional campaigning.

The campaign built a large presence on Facebook, YouTube and other digital platforms. Its own network, **My.BarackObama.com**, allowed supporters to create profiles, organize events, contact voters and raise money. Email and text messaging helped the campaign turn online enthusiasm into donations, volunteer work and voter registration.

Obama’s announcement of Joe Biden as his running mate by text message — even though the news leaked shortly before the official message — illustrated how the campaign invited supporters into a direct, technology-driven relationship.

McCain’s campaign maintained a website, used email, posted videos and engaged in online fundraising. It was not absent from the Internet. But its operation lacked the scale, integration and participatory culture of Obama’s. McCain relied more heavily on traditional media appearances, major speeches, televised debates and established Republican networks.

That difference mattered especially among younger voters, who were more likely than older Americans to encounter campaign information through friends, social networks and online video. Obama’s digital presence gave young supporters repeated opportunities to participate and to recruit one another. McCain’s online presence was more likely to communicate a message than to build a self-sustaining community around it.

## Age became part of the contrast

McCain was 72 on Election Day and would have been the oldest person elected to a first presidential term at that time. Obama was 47 and presented himself as the leader of a new political generation.

McCain’s age did not automatically disqualify him with younger voters. His military service and long Senate record earned respect, and his earlier reputation as a “maverick” had once given him some appeal beyond the Republican base. But the 2008 campaign repeatedly reinforced an image of McCain as less comfortable with the digital culture shaping younger Americans’ lives.

A frequently cited moment came when McCain acknowledged that he was not personally adept at using computers and depended on aides and family members for some Internet tasks. His opponents used comments like that to portray him as out of touch. The issue was not simply whether a president could operate a computer; it became shorthand for a wider argument about generational change, adaptability and understanding the modern economy.

Comedy programs, online clips and political advertisements amplified that image. Because younger voters were heavy consumers of shareable video and political satire, unfavorable portrayals could circulate rapidly and become part of McCain’s public identity.

## The gap was about more than technology

Political analysts caution against attributing McCain’s poor showing among voters under 30 solely to his Internet strategy or age.

Young voters were already moving toward the Democratic Party. Many opposed the Iraq war, disapproved of the Bush administration and were concerned about college costs, health care, climate change and employment. The financial crisis intensified those concerns during the final months of the campaign.

McCain also faced the burden of running as the nominee of the incumbent party at a time when President Bush was deeply unpopular. Although McCain emphasized his independent record, Obama repeatedly linked him to Republican policies of the previous eight years.

Obama, meanwhile, was a historically significant candidate whose message of “hope” and “change” was particularly effective among younger and first-time voters. His background, speaking style and emphasis on grass-roots participation helped make his campaign feel less like a conventional presidential effort and more like a youth-driven movement.

McCain’s selection of Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin briefly generated enthusiasm among conservatives and attracted intense media attention. But it did not substantially close the gap with young voters. Questions about Palin’s experience and readiness also complicated McCain’s effort to make experience a central argument against Obama.

## A disadvantage in mobilization as well as persuasion

The digital disparity affected more than voter preference. It influenced the campaigns’ ability to identify, register and mobilize younger supporters.

Obama’s online tools lowered the barrier to participation. A supporter could donate a small amount, share a video, join a local group, make calls or receive voting information from a phone or computer. That structure was especially suited to students and young workers who might not have had deep ties to traditional party organizations.

McCain had fewer comparable mechanisms for turning casual interest among younger Americans into sustained campaign activity. As a result, he faced both a **persuasion problem** — fewer young voters found his candidacy appealing — and an **organizational problem** — his campaign had less capacity to build and activate a youth constituency.

The outcome was a decisive generational split. Obama’s campaign became associated with technological fluency, diversity and political change. McCain’s campaign, fairly or not, became associated with an older political era.

In the end, McCain’s limited digital reach did not by itself cost him the election, and his age was not the only reason young voters rejected him. But together they strengthened Obama’s central argument: that the country faced a choice not just between two candidates, but between two generations and two different ways of conducting politics.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an article about McCain’s plans to win over young voters through Facebook, MySpace, college appearances, and late-night television, while highlighting Obama’s stronger youth enthusiasm.
counterfactuals.output:
# McCain Looks to Facebook, MySpace and Late-Night TV to Close Youth Gap

Sen. John McCain’s presidential campaign is stepping up efforts to win over young voters, turning to social-networking sites, college appearances and late-night television in an attempt to narrow Barack Obama’s commanding advantage among Americans under 30.

The strategy reflects both an opportunity and a challenge for McCain. Young voters have become an increasingly visible force in the election, but much of their energy has flowed toward Obama, whose campaign has used online organizing, text messaging and campus networks to attract volunteers and generate enthusiasm.

McCain’s campaign hopes to counter that momentum by meeting young Americans in the places where they spend their time. That includes expanding outreach on Facebook and MySpace, scheduling more events at colleges and universities, and placing the Arizona senator before younger television audiences through appearances on late-night programs.

The effort is intended to present McCain in a less formal setting and emphasize aspects of his record that advisers believe could appeal to younger voters. His campaign can point to his reputation for political independence, his history of challenging his own party and his support for action on climate change. McCain’s personal story—including his military service and years as a prisoner of war—also gives him a biography that may resonate beyond traditional partisan lines.

Late-night television could be particularly useful in softening McCain’s image. The senator has shown a willingness to joke about himself and engage in informal exchanges, qualities that can be harder to convey in speeches, debates and campaign advertisements. College visits likewise offer opportunities for direct conversations about tuition costs, the economy, national service, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, and other issues important to younger Americans.

But McCain faces a substantial enthusiasm gap.

Obama’s youth appeal is not based only on campaign tactics. His candidacy has become a symbol of generational and political change for many younger voters. His message, biography and opposition to the Iraq war have helped him build a following that is unusually intense for a presidential contender. Supporters have organized online, recruited friends and filled campus events, giving his campaign a level of volunteer energy that McCain has yet to match.

Obama’s campaign has also treated social networking as more than a communications tool. It has used digital platforms to turn supporters into organizers, encouraging them to create events, contact voters, raise money and share campaign material. That infrastructure gives Obama an advantage that cannot be erased simply by opening accounts on popular websites.

McCain’s task, therefore, is not merely to appear on Facebook or MySpace, but to persuade young voters that his candidacy speaks to their concerns. He must do so while balancing positions that may be unpopular with many of them, particularly his support for continuing the military effort in Iraq and his association with a Republican Party burdened by President George W. Bush’s low approval ratings.

Still, even modest gains could matter in a close election. Young people historically vote at lower rates than older Americans, and the eventual impact of Obama’s enthusiasm will depend on whether it translates into turnout. McCain’s campaign is betting that direct engagement, humor and a stronger online presence can win over independents, moderates and young voters who admire his personal history even if they disagree with parts of his platform.

The contrast is clear: McCain is working to introduce himself to a generation, while Obama is trying to mobilize one. Whether social networking, campus visits and late-night television can help McCain bridge that divide may become an important test of his campaign’s ability to compete in a rapidly changing political culture.
